The _setjmp call may be half-through with its operation when it is
interrupted by _longjmp. This can happen if iread() reaches line
172 which calls getchr, which in itself can call iread() again.
Effectively, it means that "reading" is already 1 when SET_JUMP is
called. A badly timed SIGINT could therefore mix up register states
and stack pointers of two different situations.
It can be reliably reproduced by using tmux and entering
":send-keys F C-x" to quickly send F and CTRL+x to less.
My tests on Linux/amd64 did not reveal a way to crash less or do
worse stuff, but let's be safe than sorry.
The fix is quite simple: Do not call SET_JUMP from within nested
iread calls. If reading is already 1, keep the read_label as it is.

body:
In f398927 (Use different colors for subpattern matches., 2023-01-09),
`match_pattern()` was changed so that the `sp` and `ep` pointers no
longer refer to a single start/end but to an array.
Unfortunately, the `match()` function that is used in the no-regex case
was not adjusted correctly. While it does advance `sp` and `ep` to the
next array elements in case of a match, that advancement is only visible
to the `match()` function, but not to its caller, `match_pattern()`,
which subsequently assigns `*sp = *ep = NULL`, overwriting the values
that were assigned by the  `match()` function.
As a consequence, the invariant where `search_range()` expects the
`sp`/`ep` values to be non-`NULL` if `match_pattern()` returns non-zero
is violated, and the `hilite_line()` function will call
`create_hilites()` with those invalid values and subsequently access
memory at an insanely large `start_index`, and crash.
Fix this by changing the `match()` function in a way where the `sp`/`ep`
modifications are visible to its caller.
Signed-off-by: Johannes Schindelin <johannes.schindelin@gmx.de>

value which is the first-of-two return values of a scan code.
However, there were some cases which never worked, like ungetting
any UTF-8 byte except the first (of a sequence of up to 4), where the
next WIN32getch call simply ignores the ch argument to WIN32ungetch.

body:
The trigger for this commit was to make the -D<x> mapping more
predictable. Instead of modifying win_flush (~250 LOC), the SGR
and colors logic was refactored out of win_flush, which was an
opportunity to make the logic simpler and more rebust, resulting in:
1. Apply the -D{d,s,k,u} mapping more consistently and predictably.
Previously, the -D<x> values where applied as follows:
By default (i.e. without -Da), if an SGR sequence was a single
attribute-related number, then the color was set as follows,
regardless of the attribute or the operation (set/unset):
  If BOLD is set, use the -Dd value,
  Else if INVERSE and/or ITALIC were set, use -Ds,
  Else... <same for UNDERLINE and BLINK with -Du, -Dk>
  Else, use default colors
This resulted in stateful and unpredictable application of the -D<x>
values depending on order of values and/or SGR sequence length, e.g:
  \e[0;1m            did not apply any -D value
  \e[0;33;1m         no -D value
  \e[0m\e[33m\e[1m   used -Dd (bold) value
  \e[0m\e[1m\e[33m   no -D value
  \e[0m\e[1m         used -Dd (bold) value
  \e[0m\e[1m\e[7m    also used the -Dd value... (should be -Ds ?)
  \e[0m\e[41m\e[22m  default colors instead of red bg (no attributes)
The -Da behavior ("SGR mode") had neither the -D<x> mapping nor the
stateful behavior, which resulted in much more standard and consistent
application of SGR sequences. This is still the case now.
But without -Da, the -D<x> values are now applied whenever the fg+bg
are default and exactly the relevant -D<x> attribute is set, regardless
of how it got to this state. Except for this reasonably predictable
state mapping, it's now identical to, and as consistent as "SGR mode".
This should have little negative impact in practice, if at all, because
the current behavior was likely the main use case of -D<x> in the past
too (e.g. manpage), but now it's consistent and predictable by default.
However, surely there are users which will consider this a regresion...
Note that because italic is applied as inverse (standout), previously
-Ds (standout) affected italic too. This behavior is explicitly
preserved for backward compatibility.
2. Previously, italic/inverse clashed - they shared the same bit,
   and blink/underline clashed both on their own and with the
   fg/bg/intensity - because they were not maintained independently.
E.g. \e[3;27m (set italic, unset inverse): 27 wrongly canceled 3.
Now all the attributes are maintained independently, and are applied
to Windows colors in one stateless and consistent step.
3. Additional small changes:
- Handle SGR 25 too (blink off).
- Don't treat unknown SGR values as if they were 0, e.g. \e[10m .
- Remove the difference between \e[0m and \e[0;...m (non standard).
- COMMON_LVB_UNDERSCORE no longer needs to be considered explicitly.
Potential further improvements:
- Add -Di to affect italic independently of inverse.
- Ignore or apply SGR 38/48 (256, true colors) which have extra params
  (currently 38/48 are ignored, but their additional params are not).

Restructure edit_ifile(). It now tries to open the new file first, and then if that succeeds, it closes the old (currently open) file. body:
There are three methods to support unicode file names on Windows:
1. Use the W Windows APIs (_wfopen, CreateFileW, etc). This works on
   Windows XP and later, but requires prevasive-ish code changes.
2. Attach/use a UTF-8 manifest without any code changes (i.e. keep
   using the ANSI APIs - fopen, CreateFile[A], etc). This works
   on Windows 10 1803 and later compiled with msvcrt or ucrt, can be
   done at build time or post-build, has no effect on win7/8[.1],
   but the binary doesn't run on Windows XP.
3. (try to) change the locale at runtime to UTF-8. Works on Windows 10
   1803 and later compiled with ucrt only (msvc 2015+ or mingw ucrt).
   With msvcrt and/or earlier windows this has no effect, but it runs
   on XP and later. Requires small-ish code changes, because argv/env
   are already ANSI on entry, so they need to become UTF-8.
This commit takes approach 3. If approach 1 or 2 is taken later, then
this commit can be reverted.
A UTF-8 manifest can still be used (e.g. if built with msvcrt),
at which case the new code becomes no-op (when GetACP() is CP_UTF8).

subj: use read(), not statfs(), to detect files that lie about size
body:
Files in some pseudo filesystems, particularly procfs and tracefs on
Linux, lie about their file size in stat(2). They claim to have 0 size,
but do return data when read() from.
Previously, less handled these files by using statfs(2) to check the
filesystem type (f_type field). However, there are 2 problems with this
approach:
- this requires compiling with the Linux "magic.h" header available, and
  if less is compiled without this header present, it will not have
  access to the magic numbers that define procfs and tracefs. Such a
  less binary will not work on these pseudo filesystems
- this approach is not resilient to the addition of new filesystems in
  the future with similar behavior but a new magic number
This patch takes a different approach; it takes advantage of the fact
that less (usually) read()s 256 bytes from the beginning of the file to
determine if the file is binary. The return value of the read() can be
compared with the filesize from stat(2) to determine if the latter is
This moves the bin_file() check to happen unconditionally (for regular
files, etc.), instead of only happening when the "--force" flag is
specified. While this does result in an extra syscall in that particular
circumstance, it will result in fewer syscalls overall for the most
common scenario of not specifying "--force".

subj: Do not assume PATH_MAX is defined
body:
On systems such as GNU/Hurd, PATH_MAX is not defined, because the system
intends to impose no arbitrary limits. In other systems though it might
be defined but to a very large value.
We can use realpath() with its POSIX.1-2008 semantics, where passing a
NULL argument will make it allocate the destination buffer, but not all
systems support these semantics yet.
For now, instead of complicating the code to cope with realpath()
limitations on some systems, we simply handle the case where PATH_MAX
is not defined, where realpath() should always support these semantics.

Commit ad440b6 added support for runtime UTF-8 locale, but incorrectly
documented that it's quite the same as a UTF-8 manifest, except
startup values which don't automatically become UTF-8 (like argv).
However, that's not quite true.
While the UTF-8 manifest affects all the A(NSI) Windows APIs, like
CreateFileA and fopen, the runtime setlocale method affects only
the libc/crt API, and so fopen is covered, but CreateFileA is not.
Fix the comment to mention that.
Currently "less" uses these non-libc ANSI Windows API:
- CreateFileA: only used with the ASCII name "CONIN$", so OK..
- FillConsoleOutputCharacterA: only used with spaces and other ASCII.
- ScrollConsoleScreenBufferA: same as above.
- WriteConsoleA: only used when the console CP is UTF8, so OK.
- {Get,Set}ConsoleTitleA: saves/restores the original title, and uses
  console CP regardless of manifest/locale. Will be fixed later.

body:
Previously, for SGR codes of 50 or more (e.g. ^[[38;2;150;200;250m)
the SGR processor considered it invalid sequence, and passed-through
this sequence and the rest of the current buffer (typically line).
This resulted in 256 or true color sequences passed to the terminal,
and on terminals which don't support sequences natively (i.e. before
Windows 10), this resulted in incorrect output - the sequence prints
This commit does two things:
1. Identify unknown codes exactly, rather than "code >= 50"
   (e.g. 38 is unknown, while 39 or 40 are known and supported).
2. On unknown code, don't apply more codes at this sequence.
This fixes incorrect junk output for 256/true colors on Windows
earlier than 10, e.g. as part of the content (with the -R option),
or as part of 8-bit color transformation with the -Dx options.
256/true colors still don't apply (i.e. they're ignored), but now
such sequences don't print junk.
Note that there are still sequences which the SGR processor considers
invalid, such as various OSC sequences, and more, and on these cases
the old behavior of "passthrough till the end of buffer" still apply.

subj: fix crash - buffer overflow by one in fexpand
body:
The symptom, on Windows, using LESSOPEN, was that "less" would
sometimes (up to 5-10%) crash with exit code 116.
gdb detected heap block overflow in free(filename) in lglob.
The overflow is because fexpand_copy(s, NULL) return value (and
allocated size) doesn't count the final \0, but fexpand_copy(s, x)
does write a final \0.
This appears to be a regression of commit 1626d061, where fexpand_copy
returned the strlen of the result, and fexpand allocated n+1, but
commit 1626d061 changed the allocation to n.
Fix it by always counting the \0 - which appears to fix the crash.
fexpand_copy is only used from fexpand (once to count, and once for
the actual copy), so there's no risk elsewhere from this change.

body:
To get 256/true colors working with -R (win10+ only), "sgr mode" (-Da)
should be used to bypass the internal SGR processing and passthrough
everything to the terminal directly - which can handle it on win10+.
"sgr mode" was and is working well for some releases now.
But by default (without -Da), we do internal SGR processing and apply
the values to the console outselves, including some transformation of
-D<x> values unique to windows (like underline to cyan).
In the previous release v643, the default behavior (no -Da) was:
- ANSI 8 colors SGR and attributes (1 for bold, etc) work well.
- Unknown values under 50 (like 38, 48) were processed as 0 (reset).
- SGR values of 50 or more aborted the internal SGR processor and
  switched to passthrough till the end of the current input buffer.
- On abort+passthrough, the internal SGR state was kept unmodified.
This resulted in broken behavior for 256/true colors, e.g.:
- SGR 38;5;33  was incorrectly applied as reset, blink, yellow-fg.
- SGR 38;5;50  was passthrough, and the internal state became blink.
The passthrough was clearly broken on pre-win10, as the terminal can't
handle it, but on win10+, the passthrough seems to work if not looking
too closely.
E.g. in some syntax highlighters where all the 256/true colors
include at least one value >= 50, it did appear working on win10+.
In release v661 the behavior was simplified and tightened:
- ANSI 8 colors SGR and attributes (1 for bold, etc) work well.
- Any unknown value (like 38, 48) aborts the rest of this sequence
  without passthrough (prior values at this seq, if any, do apply).
As a result, 256/true colors sequences are ignored, there's no issue
on pre-win10, we never misinterpret such sequences, never passthrough,
and the internal state is always in-sync with the actual terminal.
However, it does look like a regression compared to cases which did
appear to be working in v643.
This commit fixes this "regression", but without the downsides of v643:
- On win10+, instead of aborting the sequence on unknown values like
  v661 does, we now switch to "controlled passthrough" mode until
  reset is detected, and then switch back to the internal SGR handler.
As a result:
- On pre-win10 it's like v661 (256/true colors are ignored cleanly).
- On win10+: all 256/true colors always "work", never misinterpreted.
- The internal state is in-sync - cleared on reset after passthrough.
- Like -Da, the -D<x> transformations are skipped during passthrough.
Fixes #538

windows: SGR processor: improve end-of-buffer detection
body:
The code at win_flush expects is_ansi_end(c) to return 0 if c == 0,
but it actually returns 1.
Due to that, it could sometimes fail to detect the end of the input
buffer (which ends in \0), read past it, and sometimes crashed.
Reaching the end of the buffer (1K) was rare - only when the visible
part of an output line is generated from more than 1K bytes.
This doesn't necessarily mean that the visible part of the line spans
more than 1024 columns (although this would also be such a case), but
rather that there are many invisible bytes at the line, like escape
sequences, so that e.g. 80 or 100 columns output can be generated
from 1K string which includes many SGR escape sequences.
This commit adds a new function is_ansi_end_0 which behaves like
win_flush expects is_ansi_end to behave, and now uses it instead.
During testing with a tiny buffer (8 bytes) and many SGR escape
sequences (not bigger than 8 bytes) which trigger end-of-buffer
behavior many times for each line, no bad behavior was observed.
There remains at least one non-critical issue where if a sequence
begins at the last byte of the buffer, then the ESC is passthrough
instead of being processed as SGR, but it's un-noticeable on win10+
because the terminal handles the ESC sequence in such case.

- An sgr sequence is longer than half the buffer (512 = 1024 / 2).
- The strcpy implementation copies starting at the end backwards

Both conditions are unlikely, but still, memmove is always correct.

subj: Make SIGTSTP work as expected if received during iopen.
body:
In ca59eda0baea2409ebef33406269474d61efd93b iopen was created
which handles SIGINT received during a blocked open(). But as
noted in the commit message, SIGTSTP was handled the same as SIGINT.
This commit fixes SIGTSTP to stop the process rather than kill it.
This required changing psignals() to send SIGSTOP rather than SIGTSTP
to the current process to stop it. SIGTSTP doesn't stop the process
even though the handler is set to SIG_DFL. I don't know why, but
it seems harmless enough to use SIGSTOP rather than SIGTSTP.

subj: "waiting for data" msg should appear immediately on F command on a fifo.
body:
On a file, poll() returns POLLIN (readable data) even if we are at
end of file. This allows the code in ch_get to see that there is no
data available and display the "waiting for data" message. But on a
fifo, if there is no data available, poll() will block until the
timeout, so at eof on a pipe we will be stuck in the poll and never
display the waiting message. This commit changes the timeout so that
on the first read on a fifo (when there is no waiting message displayed)
we will use timeout=0 and return immediately. This allows ch_get to
display the waiting message. After the message is displayed,
subsequent reads will use an infinite timeout.
Related to #555.

Restructure iopen so SIGWINCH is handled like SIGTSTP:
it calls psignal to process the signal and then calls open again.
Also use sigsetjmp/siglongjmp rather than setjmp/longjmp.

signal handler. This also explains why sending a SIGTSTP signal
in psignal didn't work, so remove the now-unnecessary kludge that
sent SIGSTOP rather than SIGTSTP to the process to stop it.

body:
The -r option is very rarely useful, and can even be harmful,
in that a file containing lines longer than the screen
width will be displayed incorrectly. Also, viewing a file
containing escape sequences could put the terminal in an
unknown or unsafe condition.  The user is expected
to use -r judiciously, invoking it only when the viewed file
is known to contain "safe" content.
Therefore, it is almost always an error to put -r in the LESS
environment variable.  In all but exceedingly rare situations,
the -R option should be used instead.
This commit makes less treat any -r option in a LESS environment
variable as if it were -R. Intentional use of -r must be done
on the command line or via the - command.

Previously, prep_hilite was called in several places and would try to
prepare a largish section of the file at once. The size of the prepped
section was more or less random, depending on the size of the line buffer
at the time of the call. This was ostensibly done for "efficiency", but
it's not really much more efficient than prepping smaller sections in
several calls to prep_hilite. It has the negative side effect that
when file input was not immediately available (eg. a slow pipe), less
would get stuck in prep_hilite waiting for data, and not display data
that was already available.

a time. This avoids unnecessarily waiting for more data before displaying
data that is already available. There are also some changes specifically

long file line were displayed, each call to get_forw_line() to
get a screen line would scan backwards to the beginning of the file
line, then scan forward again back to the screen line position.

by get_forw_line(). If the next call to get_forw_line() asks for the
next contiguous screen line, we obtain the SGR sequences from the
previous line buffer so we don't need to scan backwards and forwards.

body:
Previously if an abort signal was received while reading the input
file, we would set the EOF position to the current read position.

and it causes the file to end prematurely when the user sends a
^X or ^C, or (since 23ff6a42488a9eee83341265c0c053d97b56f33d), if
the user hits any key.

still exit forw() early when receiving an input char during the
file read, but at least it doesn't ring the bell to call attention
to the early abort now. I'm not sure how to truly avoid the early
abort while still allowing any key to interrupt a file read; these
seem contradictory goals.

xn can officially mean two things, and there's no way to tell whether
the terminal behaves like one or the other:
The first interpretation, by almost all terminals, including VT100, means
the cursor stays at the last column after printing one printable char at
the last column, and only wraps to the next line (and possibly scrolls)
when an additional printable char is printed (e.g. printing a printable
char to the last column and then printing SGR sequences doesn't wrap).
The second interpretation (no terminal which I know of behaves like this),
means "if newline is printed right after it wrapped (and possibly scrolled),
then ignore this newline".
Less uses the first interpretation, so rename the variable to something
more consistent with that interpretation.

subj: Fix unexpected scrolling past end of file.
body:
Previously we stopped forward scrolling after reading EOF when the
scroll is not "forced" and the top line is not empty (a tilde).
I'm not sure why the top line clause is there. It has existed since
the earliest extant version. I guess the thinking was that it's always
safe to scroll an empty line off the top of the screen since no file
data is being lost. However this can cause unexpected scrolling
behavior. It seems better to not do a non-forced scroll past EOF
even if the first line is empty.
There was also a condition that stopped scrolling if there was only
one line displayed at the top of the screen, in order to avoid scrolling
all the content off the screen. But this duplicates a test for the
same condition in forward(), so seems redundant.
Finally, this commit allows a signal to interrupt backwards scrolling.
Previously signals were checked only in forward scrolling. It seems
less likely (perhaps impossible?) for a backwards scroll to pause
waiting for data, but it seems better to be consistent in allowing
a signal to interrupt any scroll.
Related to #720.

a digit command).
This was broken again in 04ab72cea3da04099ea70955f50152045009e93a
which fixed a problem when one command or env var is a prefix of
another, but reintroduced the bug fixed by
It also broke the --no-paste option.
This commit fixes that regression, so a longer partial match takes
precedence over a shorter exact match.
This also makes --no-paste work correctly again.

subj: Another rewrite of the command parser.
body:
The previous design split the parser into two functions, cmd_decode
which looks up a command in all command tables, and cmd_search which
looks up a command in a single table. This design required state to
be shared between the two functions, and some subtle logic to be
duplicated in each function. The design was fragile and hard to
make changes to.
This commit removes the cmd_search function. cmd_decode now does the
whole job more simply by operating on a virtual table which is the
concatenation of the individual tables. This also fixes several bugs.
The annoying part of this new design is handling the #stop directive.
Since the built-in table is parsed before any user-defined tables,
the #stop directive can't just stop parsing like it could previously;
this would allow built-in commands to be parsed. Instead, if any
user-defined table contains a stop directive, all tables besides
that one are simply ignored.
Related to #727 and #728.

subj: Fix bug when setting attributes on a --color value.
body:
tput_outmode clears a terminal attribute mode if it is currently set.
It determines whether a mode is set by testing the corresponding AT_*
bit in attrmode. These bits have historically been set by calling
at_enter with an attr value containing one or more of the 4 attribute
bits (AT_UNDERLINE, AT_BOLD, AT_STANDOUT and/or AT_BLINK).
608c8e51801a304c7398ba563402a754694f0041 added support for attribute
modifiers on a --color descriptor. However using this feature can cause
an attribute to be set in the terminal without the corresponding bit set
in attrmode. For example, at_enter could be called with
attr=AT_COLOR_LINENUM, while a --color=N-u option would set the line
number color to include underlining. In that case, after setting the
terminal to the color for line numbers, the terminal will be in
underline mode, but attrmode won't include the AT_UNDERLINE bit, and
tput_outmode will think there is no need to clear the attribute.
This fixes the problem by keeping the actual terminal attribute state in
a new variable attrbits, which is set correctly whether the attribute
is set in the "old" way or via a color descriptor.
Related to #730.

subj: V8 regexp.c: fix warnings in regdump
body:
When compiling with DEBUG defined, two ptrdiff_t values were printed
as "%d" format, which resulted in a warning in clang (but not gcc).
This was an issue in 64 bit builds, as a pointer (diff) is 64 bit
while int is typically 32.
The most correct solution would be to use %td (ptrdiff_t format),
which is not supported in c89, but we have another correct solution
which does work in c89 or later:
Use %ld and cast the value to long - which is what this commit does.
This works great for us, because eventhough int and long are typically
the same size (32 bit), long in c89 and later guarantees 32 bit, while
int in c89 or later only guarantees 16 bits.
The actual value in practice is currently limited to 32K (regcomp
aborts if regsize >= 32767), so %ld with cast to long covers our
current needs, and still allows this limit to be raised up to 2M
without breaking the correctness of this code in c89 or later.
For what it's worth, regdump works and seems useful.

subj: V8 regexp.c: move bracket handling to a function (no-op)
body:
regcomp calls regatom, which is the main regexp parser, and handling
a bracket expression was a big part of it. This made it hard to follow
the overall flow of regatom. Also, this code started at indent level 3
and reached indent level 7, which made it hard to add more code.
So just extract it to its own function regbracket(), which makes
regatom much more readable, and allows extending the brackets code
(which the next commit will do).
The change moves the actual character-handling part from regatom
to the new regbracket, while the '[' code at regatom remains only the
outer skeleton of setting up the node and finally terminating it.
The code is unmodified, but the regbracket code doesn't work on the
the global regparse anymore, and instead takes a pointer "in" to the
chars, and returns pointer to after the processed chars, so all the
instances of "regparse" at the new regbracket were renamed to "in".

This is not critically useful, because most of the classes can be
replaced trivially with normal ranges, like [a-z] for [[:lower:]],
but it's still convenient, like with [:xdigit:], or even more so
with [:punct:] which is otherwise hard to specify ([^ 0-9A-Za-z]
comes close but inconvenient, and also include control chars).
Character classes are also POSIX, so overall it's nice to have.
The implementation is fairly simple. We add an array of the chars
per class (only POSIX/C locale values), and augment regbracket()
to identify and process them during regcomp.
The code reuses the regbracket() parsing to specify the class chars
as ranges where appropriate, which is more readable and less data.
Known issue: case-insensitivity for [:upper:] doesn't work in "less".
E.g.:
  Matches all upper/lower alpha: less -I MYFILE +/"[A-Z]"
  Doesn't match anything:        less -I MYFILE +/"[[:upper:]]"
However, this is not a new issue with V8, and it also happens with
the patterns "[@-_]" or "[H-a]" etc, regardless of this commit.
A solution to this would be to support REG_ICASE or equivalent at
regexp.c, instead of "less" implemeting ICASE by doing tolower on
the pattern (regcomp) and text (regexec2) - which works for [A-Z]
but not for [[:upper:]] or [@-_] .
Other classes are unaffected because either they don't contain alpha
chars (digit, punct, cntrl), or they contain both the upper and lower
case of their alpha values (alnum, xdigit, etc) and the lower-case
chars are already included anyway. So "upper" is the exception.

subj: Don't retry read after a read error.
body:
Treat a read error as end of file, rather than automatically retrying
the read. Retrying causes less to hang on a persistent read error.
Most read errors are probably persistent anyway, so treating as EOF
is better, and the user can manually retry the read with the R
command if desired.
Even after this change, less will do several read attempts after a
read error, so only display one read error message every few seconds
to avoid a sequence of several messages in a row.
Related to #741.

subj: Replace timer for read error messages.
body:
19b689e7f57d3491b0e14380e206a01613e383f9 added a timer to limit
read error messages to 1 every 4 seconds, to avoid repeated messages
when file has a persistent read error. This change removes that
timer and simply defers read error messages until the next prompt.
This produces more deterministic behavior.
This also fixes a bug where if one of the prompt-time messages
is displayed while & filtering is in effect, the & prefix on the
prompt did not display.
Related to #741.

subj: Treat a line number of 0 in a tags file as invalid instead of crashing
body:
Ctags line numbers start from 1.
Less takes advantage of this internally by using a line number of 0 to indicate
that a tag is identified by a pattern rather than a line number.
However if the line number in a tag was actually 0 then less will get confused
and attempt to access the pattern string which, for a tag identified by a line
number, is a NULL pointer, causing a segmentation fault.
To fix this, treat any tag with a line number of 0 as invalid and skip it, as is
done for other parsing errors in tags files.
This matches the behaviour of both vim and nvi2, which both treat a line number
of 0 in a tag as an error.

body:
When F mode is interruted via ^C, psignals calls getcc_clear
to discard any pending input that was typed before the ^C.
But when ^X rather than ^C is used, there is no real signal
so psignals is not called and pending keys remain queued and
are eventually read and interpretted. To make ^X consistent
with ^C, call getcc_clear when we detect the ^X.

Then a subsequent ^X would not be seen, because WIN32getch would just return
the queued char rather than the ^X. Change the logic to pass a char* to
win32_kbhit2, which will return an ASCII input char via that char* instead
of queuing it.

body:

way. 8f107024f8a9eb005fb942b8eed2c5217c45545a fixed #752 by ensuring
that the screen is displayed before executing any commands passed in
via a + command line option. But this causes unexpected behavior when
passing an & filter command, since the initial screen will be displayed
without filtering, and then the filter will be applied later.
I originally thought that #752 might be an instance of a more
widespread problem that required all + commands to be deferred until
the initial screen is displayed. But I now think this only applies
to the m (mark) command, and it's better to force the screen to be
displayed only in that command. If other commands are discovered
that also require the screen to be displayed, those individual
commands can be fixed, but I think it's improper to make this
happen for all commands.
Related to #759.

and "opener" programs was too complicated and it was practically
impossible to write a safe handler/opener pair that did not allow
malicious URIs to execute code.
The old design was intended to allow stuffing all the logic to parse
a URI into the LESS_OSC8_xxx environment variable, to avoid the need
for a separate parsing program. This goal forced a design that was
too hard to use correctly. The new design uses just one program (called
a handler) than replaces the old handler/opener pair. The URI from the
OSC 8 link is passed to the handler program and the handler is
responsible for both parsing the URI and opening the link. If the handler
is an existing program which does not know how to parse a URI, it may be
necessary to create a wrapper handler that parses the URI and then passes
the appropriate modified value(s) to the real program.
For example, some versions of man cannot parse a string of the
form "man:cat(1)", so a wrapper is needed to convert this into an
invocation like "man 1 cat".) In the old design, this parsing was done
by the handler which returned the "opener" command line to less for
execution. In the new design, the handler does both the parsing and
the execution of the modified URI.
The special case to allow a handler starting with ":e" to open a file
in the current less instance has been removed. In most cases (such as
with file: URIs), the name of the file can't be easily extracted from
the URI without running a parser program. This case was of limited use
anyway, and tended to be confusing to the user since after opening a
file URI it was not obvious whether you are seeing the same less
instance or a new one.
A minor benefit of the new design is it is no longer necessary to
reject URIs which contain single-quote or double-quote characters.

subj: Allow lesskey mapping of keypad ENTER.
body:
Keypad ENTER is treated specially, and is converted to newline before
calling the command decoder (so that it can be used without decoding
such as at the end of entering a search string or to dismiss an error
message). This commit adds the sequence "\kpe" to map that key,
and if it is mapped, disables the low-level conversion to newline.
Also adds "noaction" as a possible line-edit action in a lesskey file.
Related to #761.

subj: Fix backwards conditional in handling keypad ENTER.
Allow OSC 8 man link with non-numeric section name.
body:
Allow an OSC 8 hyperlink to a man page to have a section name
which is not all digits, like "man:printf(3p)".

subj: Use /usr/bin/env to find bash rather than hardcoding path.
Use [[...]] rather than [...] in bash scripts.
Remove unnecessary exit status from less-osc8-file.
Fix some buffer overruns using malformed lesskey files.
Add alternate forms for shift/ctrl special keys in lesskey file.
body:
New forms use a more consistent style with "^" for control keys
and "+" for shifted keys. These are more mnemonic than the old forms.

subj: Add support for more shift/ctrl special keys.
body:
Add support for
    shift-UPARROW
    shift-DOWNARROW
    ctrl-UPARROW
    ctrl-DOWNARROW
    shift-DELETE
Also, ctrl-DELETE was previously supported on Windows but not on
terminfo-based systems, so add that to the latter.
By default, none of these keys do anything, but they can be mapped
via lesskey.

subj: Fix buffer overrun on another type of malformed lesskey file.
body:
If the last entry in a command table contains a length byte
that claims that the entry is longer than it actually is, and in fact
says that the entry extends beyond the actual end of the table,
expand_special_keys could write beyond the end of the table buffer.

subj: Make unassigned special keys do nothing.
body:
Previously some unassigned special keys would produce error beeps
or enter escape sequences into the command line.
Assign NOACTION to them so they do nothing.
Keys affected are
    ctrl-UPARROW
    ctrl-DOWNARROW
    shift-UPARROW
    shift-DOWNARROW
    DELETE
    ctrl-DELETE
    shift-DELETE
    INSERT
    BACKSPACE
    ctrl-BACKSPACE
    BACKTAB

subj: Make BS and DEL be NOACTION outside of command line.
On Windows, use simulated SIGWINCH instead of check_winch().
body:

subj: Quote references to section heading titles.
body:
The `lq` and `rq` _strings_ are universally portable to man(7) macro
packages (and mandoc(1), too).  They have a drawback, too (below), but
it's better to use them when helpful than to avoid quotation altogether.
groff_man_style(7):
   Font style macros
     ... Brief specimens of literal text, such as article titles, inline
     examples, mentions of individual characters or short strings, and
     (sub)section headings in man pages, are suitable for quotation; ...
groff_man(7):
   Strings
     The following strings are defined for use in man pages.  groff man
     supports others for configuration of rendering parameters; see
     section “Options” below.
     \*(lq
     \*(rq   interpolate special character escape sequences for left and
             right double‐quotation marks, \(lq and \(rq, respectively.
   History
     ... 4BSD (1980) added lq and rq strings. ...  Unix System V (1988)
     incorporated the lq and rq strings.
     Except for EX/EE, James Clark implemented the foregoing features in
     early versions of groff.  ...  Plan 9 from User Space’s troff ...
     incorporated the lq and rq strings in 2025.
groff_man_style(7):
Notes
     Some tips on composing and troubleshooting your man pages follow.
     • When and how should I use quotation marks?
       As noted above in subsection “Font style macros”, apply quotation
       marks to “brief specimens of literal text, such as article
       titles, inline examples, mentions of individual characters or
       short strings, and (sub)section headings in man pages”.  Multi‐
       word literals, such as Unix commands with arguments, when set
       inline (as opposed to displayed between EX and EE), should be
       quoted to ensure that the boundaries of the literal are clear
       even when the material is stripped of font styling by, for
       example, copy‐and‐paste operations.  groff, Heirloom Doctools
       troff, neatroff, and mandoc support all of the special characters
       \[oq], \[cq], \[lq], \[rq], \[aq], and \[dq] described in
       subsection “Portability” above.  DWB, Plan 9, and Solaris troffs
       do not.  Interpolating the strings \*(lq and \*(rq portably
       yields directional double quotation marks, if available, in all
       these formatters (though neatroff does not supply a man macro
       package), but they cannot reliably be used in macro arguments.

subj: Merge branch 'post700' of https://github.com/gwsw/less into post700
Don't init terminal if stdout is not a tty.
body:
If stdout is not a tty, less just cats the file to stdout.
In that case, don't call get_term() to initialize the terminal.
Also when closing the input file, don't try to save the current
position, which will crash if the position table has not been
Related to #768.

subj: less-osc8-{file,man}: use POSIX sh instead of bash
body:
bash is not guaranteed to exist by default (e.g. Alpine linux, BSDs),
and POSIX sh is both more portable and much more likely to exist and
work with the standard-ish shebang #!/bin/sh
$HOSTNAME is mostly bash-specific, so if it's missing/empty, we grab
it either from bash or from "uname -n".
Note that the new scripts are not 100% identical to the old ones:
- less-osc8-file now also supports file:///PATH .
- less-osc8-man does not test that SECTION is without parenthesis.
Valid values do work like before, but the validation is more relaxed,
though it should be good enough, so keep it simple.
If we failed to invalide, then less/man would error on invalid input.
Also, errors are improved:
- Error messages now include the argument at the end (didn't before).
- Errors now exit with code 1 (was 0).
For better integration with "less", error messages are still printed
to stdout rather than stderr, and don't include the script name which
printed the error, as requested by the maintainer.

subj: Fix minor display issues with opening OSC 8 hyperlinks.
body:
When selecting an OSC 8 link with the mouse, part of the mouse
escape sequence could appear in the command line, and then is
not erased before the OSC 8 opener is invoked. Call cmd_exec
to erase the command line before invoking the opener.
Also minor changes to default osc8 opener error messages.

subj: Fix beep when resizing window on Windows build.
body:
win32_window_event causes the next or current tty read to return
READ_AGAIN, to allow the commands() loop to break out of the read
and redraw the screen. However the command loop was then trying to
decode the READ_AGAIN as a command character. Just ignore it.
Related to #771.

subj: Don't return special keys (scan codes) from win32_kbhit2(ptr).
body:
On Windows, we call win32_kbhit2 in iread to detect whether a key has been
pressed, which should interrupt the file read if it is an interrupt key.
If it is not an interrupt key, we call win32_enqueue to push it back on
the input queue for later handling.
But scan code keys return two bytes, 0x00 followed by a PCK_* key.
Don't try to return such a key from win32_kbhit2. To make this correct,
we would need to push both chars back on the input. But a scan code key
can never be an interrupt key, so don't bother; just ignore scan code
keys in win32_kbhit2 when looking for an interrupt key.
Related to #772.

subj: Don't return non-ASCII keys from win32_kbhit2(ptr).
body:
Similar to previous commit, we should not return TRUE from win32_kbhit2
if we have merely queued a non-ASCII (UTF-8) sequence but not stored it
in *pch. This causes the call to win32_kbhit2 in iread to use an
uninitialized character as the "pressed" key.

subj: Lowercase the scheme when finding LESS_OSC8_OPEN_xxx variable.
body:
If the URI in an OSC 8 link has no colon, use the environment
variable LESS_OSC8_OPEN_NONE rather than LESS_OSC8_OPEN_
to find the handler.
If the URI in an OSC 8 link has a scheme containing uppercase
characters, convert to lowercase when finding the LESS_OSC8_OPEN_xxx
environment variable. This avoids possible conflict with the
special variables LESS_OSC8_OPEN_ANY and LESS_OSC8_OPEN_NONE.
Related to discussion in #770.

When handling an OSC 8 link, just append the shell-escaped
URI from the link to the value of the LESS_OSC8_OPEN_xxx variable.
Don't do prompt-expansion as that is unnecessarily complicated,
and makes it necessary to backslash-escape prompt metachars
like dot, colon, etc.
Related to discussion in #770.

subj: Replace less-osc8-file and less-osc8-man with less-osc8-open.
body:
Combine the scripts less-osc8-file and less-osc8-man into one
script less-osc8-open which handles both file: and man: URI.
Replace the default environment variables
    LESS_OSC8_OPEN_file = less-osc8-file
    LESS_OSC8_OPEN_man = less-osc8-man
with
    LESS_OSC8_OPEN_ANY = less-osc8-open
Related to discussion in #770.

subj: Fix bug in mouse clicking OSC 8 link that crosses a screen line.
body:
If an OSC 8 link is clicked in a long line that wraps across more
than one screen line, previously osc8_click would call osc8_search_line
and tell it to search for the selected link only within the screen line
that was clicked. If the link started in the previous line,
osc8_search_line we would not see the start of the OSC 8 sequence,
so it would not find the link.
Instead, tell osc8_search_line to start searching at the start of the
line in the file, rather than the start of the line on the screen.
Related to #775.

subj: Set EOF when jumping to end of file even if filtering.
body:
jump_forw() seeks to EOF and then scrolls backwards to fill the screen.
If input is being filtered, the soft_eof position should track the end
of filtered input, so set it in jump_forw.
This ensures that "END" will appear in the prompt line after a
G command even if input is filtered.
Related to #774.

subj: Fix missing bell when jump to end with & filter in effect.
body:
When an & filter is active, pressing G jumps to the end of the
(filtered) input. Pressing G again should ring the terminal bell,
but does not do so if the last line of the file is filtered out.
This commit fixes that.

subj: Display OSC 8 links in underline mode, and add -DO to change this.
body:
To make it easier to identify displayed OSC 8 links, print each OSC 8
link in underline mode by default.
The -DO option can be used to change the attributes of OSC 8 links.

subj: Simplify clearing wrapped OSC 8 link at end of line.
body:
Don't need both hlink_in_line and in_osc8_link variables.
The new in_osc8_link can be used to determine whether we need to
emit a null OSC 8 sequence at end of line, and is actually better
than using the old hlink_in_line since the latter emits the null
sequence if any link appears anywhere in the line, while the former
emits the null sequence only if we are actually in the middle of
a link.

subj: Fix two display issues related to OSC 8 link underlining.
body:
1. When storing an underlined char in an OSC 8 link, need to treat the
underlining separate from search hiliting. Search hiliting should set
in_hilite and the end of search hiliting should (if in_hilite is set)
resend the last 3 escape sequences, to restore color that was
interrupted by the search hilite. But OSC 8 underlining is
orthogonal to coloring, doesn't interrupt it, and end of underlining
shouldn't resend escape sequences.
2. Don't save OSC 8 sequences as sequences that might need to be
resent. It is not necessary and since OSC 8 sequences tend to be long
(since they contain a URL), it is wasteful.

subj: Merge branch 'post700' of https://github.com/gwsw/less into post700
More fixes for OSC 8 link display.
body:
After end of OSC 8 text, need to resend the last escape sequence.
This isn't necessary if the OSC 8 text is just underlined (the
default), but if the OSC 8 highlight was changed to a real color
via the -DO option, the color from the escape sequences in the
file needs to be restored.

subj: Make selected OSC 8 links be underlined as well as highlighted.
body: This helps distinguish a selected OSC 8 link from a search match.

subj: Loosen the syntax requirements for color descriptors a little.
body:
1. Previously a descriptor that specified an attribute (bold,
underline, etc.) but left color unchanged required a "-" as the color.
Now the color part can be omitted entirely. So for bold line numbers,
you can use "-DNd" instead of "-DN-d".
2. Allow a dot followed by an empty background color in 6-bit
descriptors; eg. "-DN43.".

subj: Remove deprecated lesskey program; fix build if USERFILE is undefined.
body:
The lesskey program has been deprecated since less-582.
Now we will stop building and distributing it.

subj: Fix build with Watcom C compiler.
Add some comments to code related to UTF-8 handling.
Fix some issues if shell_quote() returns NULL.
body:
The only way shell_quote() can return NULL is if DEF_METAESCAPE is
defined to be an empty string, and the user opens a file containing
a quote character. DEF_METAESCAPE is empty only on Windows and OS/2.
However when opening a filename containing a quote on Windows,
somehow the quote is replaced with U+F022. I don't know how this
happens, but this seems to make it impossible to actually cause any
of these bugs to occur on either Linux or Windows without modifying
the code to make shell_quote return a NULL.
Regardless, for safety, we now check for shell_quote() returning a
NULL in all of its invocations.

subj: Add %G, %y and %% expansions in prompt strings.
Fix unsafe handling of unterminated OSC sequence.
body:
If file contains an unterminated OSC sequence, previously we added
an ST terminator at end of line. This is unsafe; instead just remove
the entire sequence.

subj: Fix a few signedness mismatch issues.
body: Related to #782.

subj: Use custom version of shell_quoten for Windows.
body:
Adapted from https://github.com/rmyorston/busybox-w32/blob/f9e24f4766afdf2c0a1011097bd2fd6e01fd39e0/win32/process.c#L115-L150
Discussed in #784.

subj: Make # and % expandion in :e and ! commands be shell-escaped.
body:
The special chars '#' and '%' are expanded to filenames.
We should shell-escape those filenames for safety.
Related to #784.

subj: Fix compiler warnings when using TO_UPPER and TO_LOWER.
Make raw_mode parameter be lbool not int.
On Windows, don't reset signal handlers while running a subprocess.
body:
On Windows, a signal such as ctrl-C received while less runs a subprocess
is also received by the dormant less parent, and therefore kills it.

subj: Fix lesskey problem in overriding a command with a longer command.
body:
An attempt by a lesskey file to define a command with a prefix matching
a complete preexisting command would fail. This commit makes it possible
do this, but the preexisting command must first be redefined as "invalid".
Related to #795.

subj: Add environment variable cache in case getenv returns a volatile string.
body:
The POSIX spec says that the value returned from getenv could be
overwritten by a subsequent call to getenv. The less code assumes
that this is not the case, and that the value returned from getenv
has an indefinite lifetime. Fixing the various individual uses of
getenv would be tedious and error-prone, so just add a cache to
ensure that lgetenv returns a value with indefinite lifetime,
even if getenv does not.
I am not aware of any system on which getenv actually returns a
volatile value, so this cache code is unnecessary on most (all?)
systems. The cache can be disabled by defining GETENV_NONVOLATILE,
although we currently don't do this since I don't know of a way
to reliably detect whether getenv returns a volatile value or not.

subj: Merge branch 'post700' of https://github.com/gwsw/less into post700

body:
We must get the value of POSIXLY_CORRECT using getenv not lgetenv,
because POSIXLY_CORRECT should be considered true if it is set to
any value, even an empty string, but lgetenv returns NULL if it is
set to an empty string.
This was broken in 6f498e33fafea29e756d29d4b45a807b1900d3d8.

subj: Add J, K and Y commands to help screen.
body: Related to #796.

subj: Exit with a failure status in more cases
body:
The following conditions are fatal, yet less currently handles them
by returning a success status. Return a failure status instead.
* Missing input filename when stdin is a terminal.
* Missing option argument (e.g. `less -b`).
* Not being able to open any input files in non-interactive mode
  (note that in interactive mode, this already returns a failure status).
This reverts commit 8234e0cd5faf76a7c50a85959b83e6de2c25d4af.

fd09752779d4e6954fc2d8de59e5d97435fa148a allowed a lesskey file
to invalidate a command in order to override it with a longer command
(that is, where the original command is a prefix of the longer command).
This commit makes it possible to override a command with a longer one
without the need to manually invalidate the original command.
Related to #795.
There's a simpler way to do this, coming in next commit.

04ab72cea3da04099ea70955f50152045009e93a fixed #626 by making a
full match for a command override a later partial match.
However, in a command table (as opposed to an env var table),
if a command is a prefix of a later command, the later command
should indeed be the one we match. If this case happens, the user
has deliberately overridden a command with a longer one, so we
should take the later longer one and ignore the earlier shorter one.
04ab72cea3da04099ea70955f50152045009e93a was trying to fix a
problem with env var tables, which should be treated differently:
with env vars, only exact matches matter, so we should take an
earlier exact match rather than a later partial match.
This commit changes 04ab72cea3da04099ea70955f50152045009e93a so that
we ignore a later partial match only if we are looking at an env var
table, but we ignore an earler exact match if we are looking at a
command table. At the time 04ab72cea3da04099ea70955f50152045009e93a
was made, cmd_decode did not take an "anchored" parameter, so we
had no way to know which kind of table we were looking at.
Related to #795.

subj: The ' command (goto-mark) should not modify the mark.
body:
The ' command with a numeric argument N will permanently modify the
mark to place it on line N, so that future ' commands without a numeric
argument will continue to place the mark on line N. The N should apply
only to the current command and not modify the mark for future commands.
Related to #799.

This variant of the | command reads two mark characters
and pipes the section of the file between them.
It does not extend the section to include the current screen
like the single-char | form does.

In the | and || command, ^N allows entering a line number
instead of a mark letter.
